01.n: The Greek puts the verb first: 'came the Son of Man'. English order is used here.

02.r: Part of the title, the Son of Man.

03.r: Part of the title Jesus uses of himself.

04.r: The article before 'man' in the title; English leaves it out.

05.r: Completes the title, the Son of Man.
05.n: Literally 'the son of the man'. This study renders the title 'the Son of Man' throughout.

06.r: He eats ordinary meals with people.
06.n: A present participle, describing his way of life.

08.r: He drinks, wine included, at those meals.

10.r: His critics' verdict, in the present tense.

12.r: The critics describe him as a man of a certain kind.

13.r: One who eats too much: the critics' insult.
13.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from φαγεῖν, the aorist of the verb 'eat', and records it only here and once in Luke.

15.r: One given to wine: the second insult.
15.n: Abbott-Smith builds it from οἶνος, wine, and πότης, a drinker, and defines it as 'a wine-drinker, wine-bibber'; he records one use in the Septuagint, in Proverbs. The BSB's 'drunkard' makes explicit the excess the insult implies.

16.r: The company he keeps, named first among his offences.
16.n: The Greek puts this word before 'friend': 'of toll collectors a friend, and of sinners'. This study renders the word 'toll collector' throughout.

17.r: One on close terms with them.
17.n: Abbott-Smith gives the active sense 'loving, friendly' and, as a noun, 'a friend'.

19.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse among the plural uses of the word.

20.r: Sets Jesus' answer against the critics' verdict.
20.n: The Greek has the plain word 'and'. The KJV, Geneva and BSB read it as a contrast, 'But'.

21.r: Wisdom is shown to be in the right.
21.n: An aorist passive, 'was justified'; the YLT keeps the past tense. Most translations use the present, reading the aorist as a general truth, which is a fair reading but not the only one. Abbott-Smith notes that in the Septuagint the verb chiefly translates Hebrew צָדַק in its causative stems.

22.r: Greek uses the article with abstract nouns like wisdom; English does not.

23.r: Wisdom, spoken of as a person with offspring or deeds of her own.
23.n: Abbott-Smith notes that in the Septuagint it chiefly translates Hebrew חׇכְמָה. That wisdom here stands for God's own wisdom is a reasonable reading, but it is an inference.

24.r: The source of the proof: her works show her right.
24.n: Literally 'from'. The proof comes from what wisdom does.

26.r: What wisdom does, by which she is proved right.
26.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'work, task, employment'. The KJV, Geneva, DRC and YLT read 'her children' here instead; see the note on the text.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus does not have ἔργων, 'works', at the end of the verse. The KJV, Geneva and YLT read 'her children' there, so their Greek had a word for children in its place; the ASV and BSB follow 'works'.
